title: Milder with others
hookLine: look at your own faults and you'll be gentler with others' (On Anger 2.28)

lines: LAWYER FOR ME, JUDGE FOR YOU.
cards: Someone cuts you off in traffic, and you're furious: who drives like that? Ten minutes later you drift into the next lane without signaling, and somehow that was different. You were in a hurry.
You had a reason. We are expert lawyers for ourselves and stern judges of everyone else. In the second book of On Anger, Seneca offers a cure that has nothing to do with breathing or waiting.
It's a kind of honesty: turn the light you shine on others back on yourself.

teach.h: NONE OF US IS WITHOUT FAULT.
teach.b: First, nobody is innocent. If we want to judge fairly, Seneca says, let's first agree that none of us is without fault. Examine yourself honestly and you won't find a person who could be acquitted of everything.

Second, eyes in front, faults behind. We keep other people's faults before our eyes, he says, and our own behind our back. His examples: a tyrant angry at a murderer, a temple robber punishing a theft.
Third, the softening. This isn't meant to make you feel worse about yourself. It's meant to make you gentler.
When you remember you've done something similar, the anger loses its footing.
You'll say: I've done this too. And you'll be milder. Fourth, a neighbor.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus asks in the King James words: why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?

A speck of sawdust and a plank. Two teachers of the same century, in the same empire, from very different places, reaching for the same kind of picture. Neither borrowed from the other, as far as we know.
The insight seems to arrive on its own, wherever people are honest about how they judge.

how: Some readers of Seneca pause before judging someone to recall a similar fault of their own, as a way to soften anger into fairness.

games.q: a coworker misses a deadline and you're about to complain loudly. what does Seneca suggest first?
o: remember a time you missed one too.
games.why: look behind your own back first; remembering your faults makes you milder with others'.

practice: Think of someone who annoyed you recently and name what they did, plainly.
Then gently look behind your own back for a time you did something in the same family, late, careless, short-tempered, and hold the two side by side without punishing yourself.
Notice whether the anger toward them softens, even a little.

wordCard.voice: Vitia. Latin for faults, vices, which, Seneca says, we keep in front for others and behind for ourselves. Turn around, and you'll judge more gently. Today's word.
